rationale: Start with a broad gradient to maximize the chance of observing all 10 compounds while surveying retention and critical separations. A midrange temperature leaves room to tune selectivity in either direction.

Halve the gradient duration to reduce the time penalty while testing how much of the substantial resolution margin is retained. Keeping the endpoints and temperature fixed isolates the effect of gradient steepness.
Keep the fast gradient and increase temperature to probe selectivity in the crowded middle peaks. This tests whether their resolution can improve without reintroducing a substantial time penalty.

Slightly lengthen the gradient to improve the remaining close separation while keeping the last peak near the zero-time-penalty region. This also checks whether the other middle-peak separations remain adequate as gradient selectivity shifts.

Slightly flatten the gradient to improve the 1.59-resolution pair while testing whether the closest pair remains above 1.5. The modest retention increase may still preserve zero time penalty, providing an alternative method at the maximum CRF.

The maximum CRF is already achieved; test a slightly higher starting organic fraction for a faster alternative. This probes whether retention can decrease while maintaining resolution of both close middle-peak pairs.

Flatten the gradient slightly to restore the deficient middle-pair resolution while retaining the faster start from injection 6. This may yield another maximum-score method with a larger margin for the other close pair.

A further small reduction in gradient steepness should lift the 1.47-resolution pair above 1.5 while preserving the other close separation. The last peak is expected near 8 minutes, testing an alternative maximum-score method at the edge of the zero-time-penalty region.

Combine a higher starting organic fraction with a shallower gradient to seek better-balanced resolution of the two close pairs. Injection 8 suggests this tradeoff may preserve full separation with the last peak near the zero-time-penalty boundary.

Probe temperature sensitivity around the maximum-score method from injection 4. Lowering temperature by 5 °C will test whether its two marginal separations can be better balanced without a time penalty.

The maximum score is already secured, so test a distinct low-temperature selectivity regime with the fast gradient. Cooling may separate the crowded middle peaks through an elution-order change while keeping the last peak near the zero-time-penalty region.

Test a faster gradient at the highest temperature to explore a possible selectivity reversal among the close middle peaks. This seeks a shorter maximum-score alternative; the established CRF 1.000 method remains the benchmark.

Raise the starting organic fraction to test whether the reversed close pair at 60 °C separates further while shortening retention. The other separations in injection 12 provide some margin for this change.

Increase the starting organic fraction further to exploit the improving close-pair separation seen at 60 °C. This tests a substantially faster alternative while checking that the early peaks remain resolved.

Test whether a steeper gradient increases separation of the reversed close pair at 60 °C, while restoring the low starting organic fraction to protect early-peak resolution. This explores a faster alternative to the established maximum-score method.

Preserve injection 4’s successful gradient slope and temperature while lowering the final organic fraction and shortening the programmed gradient. Since all peaks previously eluted before this new gradient ends, this method should reproduce the maximum CRF of 1.000.

Use a gradient slope between injections 7 and 8 to target resolution above 1.5 for both close pairs, with the last peak below 8 minutes. This could provide another maximum-score method with a better balance of resolution and time margins.

Preserve the proven gradient slope from injections 4 and 16 while ending the programmed gradient sooner at a lower organic fraction. All peaks should elute before the gradient ends at the outlet, so the maximum CRF should be retained.

Keep the proven initial gradient slope but switch to a hold after the first nine peaks have eluted. This tests whether a lower final organic fraction still elutes the last compound within the zero-time-penalty window, preserving the maximum CRF.

Match injection 8’s starting composition, gradient slope, and temperature while lowering the endpoint. Because its last peak eluted before the new gradient reaches its endpoint at the outlet, this should retain CRF 1.000 and its slightly larger minimum-resolution margin.

Test a slightly shallower gradient than injection 20 to map the maximum-score region around the higher-starting-organic method. The observed trends suggest both close pairs may remain above 1.5 while the last peak stays within the demonstrated zero-time-penalty window.

Use a shallower gradient to recover the deficient separation seen at this starting composition in injection 9. This tests whether its stronger separation of the other close pair can yield a better-balanced maximum-score method without a time penalty.

Slightly flatten the gradient from injection 22 to raise its remaining deficient separation above 1.5. The last peak is expected near 9 minutes, testing whether improved resolution can still retain the maximum CRF without a time penalty.

Slightly flatten injection 21’s gradient to test the slower edge of its maximum-score region. Both close pairs are expected to remain above 1.5, with the last peak still below the approximately 9-minute zero-time-penalty boundary.

Use a gradient slope between injections 21 and 24, both of which achieved the maximum CRF, with a lower final organic fraction. This should retain full resolution and zero time penalty, providing another maximum-score alternative for the final injection.
